title: Shloka 164
subtitle: Expert at hauling out the mired, and every role in the sacrifice at once

namas.gloss: Expert At Raising Those Sunk In The Mire Of Rebirth
namas.translation: Hauling the sunk up out of where they have sunk is a skill, and she has it completely. The name fills the whole first line of its verse: those it rescues are stuck fast in saṃsāra as in mud, and she is not merely willing to pull them out but expert at it.

morphology.note: Printed nāmāvalīs often shorten this to samuddharaṇapaṇḍitā for the salutation. The stotra gives it in full, and that longer form is used here as the citation form.

compound.gloss: skilled in raising up those sunk in the mire of rebirth

children.gloss: the mud of transmigration — saṃsāra, the round of rebirth, as paṅka, mire
drawing well up, raising out, rescue

namas.translation: The offering fire pleases her, and she comes willingly wherever a rite is carried out properly.

compound.gloss: to whom the sacrifice is dear

namas.translation: She is not only the one the rite honours but the one carrying it out, acting through the priest's hands.

children.gloss: she who does or makes, the agent

namas.translation: The patron who commissions the rite and bears its cost is also her, so offering, priest and patron collapse into a single presence.

morphology.note: The possession sits in the suffix -in, so yajamānasvarūpa is the compound and svarūpiṇī a derivative of it; the bahuvrīhi reading, she who has the sacrificer for her form, is equally current.

commentary.meaning: The whole first line is a single name, sixteen syllables long, which is something the hymn almost never does. It describes people sunk in the mire of transmigration, and it says that lifting them out of it is a thing she is expert at. The word at the end of that long compound is worth pausing on: paṇḍitā, learned, skilled, professionally competent. Rescue is presented not as pity but as a craft. The second line then puts three names of the sacrifice side by side, and between them they occupy every position the rite has. The offering is dear to her, so she is the deity who receives it; she performs it, so she is the priest whose hands move; and she is the patron on whose behalf it is undertaken and who owns its fruit. The two lines belong together because in the world the hymn is written from, the sacrifice is the standard machinery for getting from where one is to somewhere better. Having named her as the one who lifts people out, the verse identifies her with the entire apparatus by which lifting out is normally attempted.
commentary.history:
Saṃsāra is sam plus √sṛ, to flow: a flowing together, a wandering through, the running of a life on and on through births. The previous verse ended with sudhāsṛti, the flowing of nectar, built on that same root √sṛ. The two words are next to each other in the recitation and are the same motion described twice, once as the circulation that will not stop and once as the outpouring that does not run out. Whether the poet intended the echo cannot be shown, but a reciter who says the two verses in sequence will hear it.

Paṅka is mud, and specifically the kind that grips. It is not the neutral word for earth or clay but the mire of a churned road or the bottom of a drying tank, and its literary force is that a creature in it cannot get purchase to escape. The same noun sits inside paṅkaja, the commonest Sanskrit word for a lotus, which means simply mud-born — the flower this goddess is repeatedly seated on takes its name from the substance this name says people are drowning in. Nirmagna, from ni plus √majj, means sunk right under, and the root's other derivative is majjana, the ordinary word for a ritual bath. Sanskrit uses one verb for immersion that purifies and immersion that kills.

Samuddharaṇa is sam plus ud plus √hṛ, a carrying up and out, and the Gītā uses the agent noun from the same three elements when Kṛṣṇa promises to become the lifter-out for those whose minds have entered him. The difference in the two images is instructive. The Gītā speaks of an ocean, where the danger is depth and the rescue is buoyancy; the hymn speaks of mud, where the danger is adhesion and the rescue is traction. The Gītā also, elsewhere, tells a man to lift himself by himself and says that the self is its own friend and its own enemy. Against that, the hymn's word paṇḍitā quietly concedes that the operation requires a specialist.

That word is the oddest thing in the verse. Paṇḍita is the ordinary term for a learned man, someone who has mastered a discipline, and its application to the work of salvation makes deliverance sound like grammar or surgery — a body of technique in which one can be more or less accomplished. The commentators generally take it in the weaker sense of clever or skilful, but the stronger reading is available and is more interesting: she is not merely willing to pull people out, she is good at it, and the difference between willingness and expertise is the difference between a rescuer and a rescue service.

The three yajña names then do something the Vedic tradition had already done to itself. The Puruṣa hymn of the Ṛgveda ends by saying that the gods sacrificed the sacrifice with the sacrifice, collapsing the offering, the offered and the act into one another; the Gītā has Kṛṣṇa declare in a single verse that he is the rite, the oblation, the formula, the clarified butter, the fire and the act of offering. What this hymn adds is the yajamāna. That word is a present middle participle of √yaj, and the middle voice is the whole point: it means the one sacrificing on his own behalf. In the solemn ritual the yajamāna is technically the sacrificer even though the priests perform nearly every action; he is the one consecrated for the rite, he bears its cost, and its merit accrues to him. He is, in other words, the only person in the enclosure who has something at stake. To call her yajamānasvarūpiṇī is to say that even that position — the beneficiary, the one with an interest — is hers.

There is a historical reason these names matter beyond their content. Śrīvidyā as it developed in South India took pains to present itself as continuous with Vedic orthodoxy rather than opposed to it, and the strand of the tradition that prevailed there argued its case partly by pointing to material of exactly this kind. A hymn embedded in a Purāṇa, spoken by Hayagrīva to Agastya, which declares the goddess to love sacrifice and to be the sacrificer, could be recited by brahmins who would not have handled a tantra. The next verse continues in the same direction, and the two together are among the reasons this text travelled where other Śākta literature did not.
commentary.practice:
This verse is unusual to recite because its first half is one name. Sixteen syllables run from saṃsāra to paṇḍitā without a break for sense, and the caesura that normally divides an anuṣṭubh here falls in the middle of a compound, between nirmagna and samuddharaṇa. Take the breath there anyway — the metre requires it — but do not let the pause turn into a boundary, because the words on either side of it are governed by each other.

A note about what you will see printed. Most namāvalīs give this as a single offering, oṃ saṃsārapaṅkanirmagnasamuddharaṇapaṇḍitāyai namaḥ, and that is the form generally recited. Listings that shorten it to samuddharaṇapaṇḍitā, as this one does, are abbreviating for the sake of a manageable label rather than recording a different reading; the qualifier is part of the name.

The consonants in that long compound are worth taking one at a time. Saṃ has an anusvāra before a sibilant, which means the nasality is carried in the vowel rather than closed off by a consonant. Paṅka is the velar nasal followed by k. Nirmagna ends in gn, a velar stop followed by a dental nasal, a cluster English never produces at all — hold the g closed and release it directly into the n. Samuddharaṇa contains a doubled d followed by an aspirated dh: ud plus dhara, so the tongue stays at the teeth through d, d and dh, and only the last of the three carries breath. And paṇḍitā is two retroflexes in contact, ṇ and ḍ, with the tongue curled well back for both.

The second line hammers on ya. Yajñapriyā, yajñakartrī, yajamānasvarūpiṇī — and the third one breaks the pattern it seems to be following, since it is yaja- and not yajña-, and it is longer than the other two put together in the recitation. Reciters who let momentum carry them often produce a fourth yajña- that is not there.

The conjunct ñ in yajña is the one sound in this verse on which practice genuinely differs by region: it is commonly heard as gy in the North, dny in Maharashtra, and something like gnya in the South. The phonetic value described by the grammarians is straightforward — the palatal stop j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made with the body of the tongue against the hard palate. Adopt whichever your teacher uses, but know what the letters say.

The four offerings are saṃsārapaṅkanirmagnasamuddharaṇapaṇḍitāyai namaḥ, yajñapriyāyai namaḥ, yajñakartryai namaḥ, yajamānasvarūpiṇyai namaḥ. The first of those is among the longest single utterances in the whole thousand and should be practised on its own before it is met in sequence.

What the verse asks of the person saying it is a double placement. The first line describes you: sunk, stuck, unable to get traction. The last name describes you as well, since the yajamāna is whoever undertakes a rite for his own benefit, and that is precisely what a person reciting a thousand names for a stated purpose is doing. The verse tells you that both the one in the mud and the one commissioning the rescue are her.

crossReferences.deva: तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् । भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: teṣām ahaṃ samuddhartā mṛtyusaṃsārasāgarāt | bhavāmi na cirāt pārtha mayy āveśitacetasām ||
crossReferences.translation: For those whose thought has entered into me I become, before long, the lifter-out from the ocean of death and transmigration, Pārtha.
crossReferences.relevance: The same verb, sam-ud-√hṛ, in the same office, and it supplies the agent noun that this name turns into a skill. The difference of image is the thing to notice: the Gītā's danger is an ocean, the hymn's is mud. It also supplies a condition — those whose minds have entered him — where the hymn supplies only a competence, which is why the two texts feel differently weighted even when they say nearly the same thing.

crossReferences.deva: यज्ञेन यज्ञमयजन्त देवास्तानि धर्माणि प्रथमान्यासन् । ते ह नाकं महिमानः सचन्त यत्र पूर्वे साध्याः सन्ति देवाः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yajñena yajñam ayajanta devās tāni dharmāṇi prathamāny āsan | te ha nākaṃ mahimānaḥ sacanta yatra pūrve sādhyāḥ santi devāḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: With the sacrifice the gods sacrificed the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those powers reached the vault of heaven, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, are.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest statement of the collapse that yajñapriyā, yajñakartrī and yajamānasvarūpiṇī perform. Instrument, object and agent of the rite are the same thing here, stated in a single line, and the verse is old enough that the identification cannot be dismissed as later tantric extravagance. The hymn is not innovating; it is applying a Vedic move to a goddess.

crossReferences.deva: अहं क्रतुरहं यज्ञः स्वधाहमहमौषधम् । मन्त्रोऽहमहमेवाज्यमहमग्निरहं हुतम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: ahaṃ kratur ahaṃ yajñaḥ svadhāham aham auṣadham | mantro 'ham aham evājyam aham agnir ahaṃ hutam ||
crossReferences.translation: I am the rite, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the healing herb; I am the formula, I am the clarified butter, I am the fire, I am the act of offering.
crossReferences.relevance: The nearest thing in the older literature to what the second line of this verse is doing, and a useful measure of what the hymn adds. The Gītā enumerates the objects and the acts of the ritual; the sahasranāma names the persons, and includes the yajamāna, the patron with an interest in the outcome. That is the one role Kṛṣṇa's list here does not claim.

references.title: The Broken World of Sacrifice: An Essay in Ancient Indian Ritual
references.author: J. C. Heesterman (University of Chicago Press, 1993)
references.note: The best book in English on what the yajamāna actually is and why the solemn ritual needed a patron who does almost nothing. Heesterman argues that the classical rite was built by removing conflict and risk from an older and messier one, which makes yajamānasvarūpiṇī a much stranger name than it looks.

references.title: Cooking the World: Ritual and Thought in Ancient India
references.author: Charles Malamoud, tr. David Gordon White (Oxford University Press, 1996)
references.note: A collection of essays, several of them on the vocabulary of the sacrifice, written with more literary intelligence than almost anything else in the field. Read the essays on the remainder and on the sacrificer's body if you want to feel the weight of the three yajña names rather than merely construe them.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: Explains the historical situation this verse belongs to: how a tantric tradition in the South argued its own Vedic legitimacy, and what it had to emphasise in order to do so. Names like yajñapriyā are part of that argument, and Brooks lets you see the argument being made.

references.title: The Purāṇas
references.author: Ludo Rocher (Harrassowitz, A History of Indian Literature, 1986)
references.note: The reference survey of the Purāṇic corpus, including the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa in which this hymn is embedded. Rocher is scrupulous about what can and cannot be dated, which is a useful corrective to the confident chronologies found in devotional editions.
